prompt: Your chat app adopts end-to-end encryption using the lesson's local-search design and WhatsApp-style pairwise client fan-out for one-to-one messages. Which consequences must the design handle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Message search must run on the device, because the server can't index ciphertext.
options.explanation: Correct. The server never has plaintext, so ordinary plaintext indexing is unavailable. This design uses local search; specialized encrypted-search protocols are outside this lesson.

options.text: Push notifications can't include message text in clear; send a generic or encrypted payload and let the app decrypt locally.
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise the content would pass through the push provider in plaintext, defeating end-to-end encryption.

options.text: Each of a recipient's devices has its own keys, so a message to a user with three devices is encrypted (at least) three times.
options.explanation: Correct. That's how WhatsApp's multi-device design works: the sender encrypts per device.

options.text: The server must decrypt messages to assign per-conversation sequence numbers.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sequence numbers are metadata the server assigns to the envelope; it doesn't need the content to order messages.
Incorrect. Receipts are acks and cursors over message IDs and sequence numbers, which the server can see without reading content.

workedExample:
Ask what the server needs to *read* for each feature:

| Feature | Needs plaintext? |
|---|---|
| Routing, seq, receipts | No (metadata) |
| Search | Yes → on device |
| Notification text | Yes → on device |
| Multi-device | Per-device keys |

E2EE shifts work onto clients and leaves the server routing and storing opaque blobs.

link.title: Meta engineering: how WhatsApp enables multi-device capability
